text.en: Gandhi wrote that he wanted the cultures of all lands to blow freely through his house, but he refused to be blown off his feet by any. India's culture in the 13th-17th centuries was like that.

Despite invasions and unstable politics, Indian culture continued and grew richer by taking in new ideas.
Traders and settlers from Greece, Persia, Central Asia and East Asia brought food, fashion, art, language and religion, and many assimilated into Indian society.
The bhakti movement stressed devotion to God over rituals, with saints like Kabir, Nanak, Mirabai, Tukaram, Chaitanya and Basaveshwara.
Sufi saints preached love and equality, and shrines such as Ajmer drew people of all faiths.
Sikhism was founded by Guru Nanak and teaches one God, equality and service.
Regional languages like Hindi, Bengali, Marathi, Telugu, Tamil and Urdu grew with devotional poetry and literature.
Amir Khusrau blended Persian and Indian music and poetry and is linked to the development of the sitar and qawwali.
Temples like Ramappa in Telangana, Vijayanagara's Hampi, and Mughal miniature painting show the arts flourishing.
New foods, fabrics and customs mixed, as in the 15th-century cookbook Ni'matnama with its paintings, showing everyday life.
Common patterns were continuation of traditions, assimilation of new ideas and new creative forms.

prompt.en: How did culture grow during unstable times?

points.en: Indian culture continued and enriched itself by assimilating ideas.
Bhakti and Sufi saints spread love, equality and devotion.
Regional languages, music, architecture and painting flourished.
